passage: The first time I volunteered at the community kitchen near the railway colony, I arrived with a plan to reorganise everything. I'd read about kitchens abroad and had ideas. Vidya-akka, who had run it for eleven years, let me talk for five minutes. Then she handed me an apron and said, 'Chop onions today, Lakshmi. Talk to people tomorrow.' I was a bit offended. But over the next month I learned why they served lunch at two, not twelve: most of the people came after morning shifts. My brilliant plans would have broken things. Now I help with the accounts, which is actually useful. I still catch myself wanting to be thanked. I'm trying to notice that and just show up.

qa.q: How long had Vidya-akka run the community kitchen?
qa.a: She had run it for eleven years.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi admit about wanting to be thanked?
qa.a: Lakshmi admits still wanting praise at times, which shows awareness of that ego.

qa.q: What made Vidya-akka's instruction wise?
qa.a: It made Lakshmi learn how the kitchen actually worked before trying to change it.

qa.q: How might the people eating at the kitchen see volunteers like early Lakshmi?
qa.a: They might see eager outsiders who don't understand their routines and could accidentally make things harder.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer learning to listen and serve without assuming they know best.

passage:
Coordinator's note, Aditi, evening literacy classes, Saturday.

Jasleen, a college student, joined us three weeks ago. On her first evening she spoke slowly and loudly to the women in class, as if they were children, and took photos of them for her college project without asking. I spoke to her privately. She went pink and apologised, and deleted the photos in front of me. Since then she has changed noticeably. She now asks the learners what they want to read. Last week one woman wanted to read her bus route signs, so Jasleen made cards with the stop names. She told me she'd stopped thinking of it as 'helping' and more as working alongside them. I have asked her to help plan next month's sessions.

qa.q: What did one woman want to read?
qa.a: She wanted to read her bus route signs.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when Aditi spoke to her, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and sorry; she went pink, apologised and deleted the photos.

qa.q: What change in Jasleen's approach made her more useful?
qa.a: She began asking learners what they wanted, such as making bus stop cards, instead of deciding for them.

qa.q: How might the women in class have felt on Jasleen's first evening?
qa.a: They may have felt talked down to and uncomfortable being photographed without being asked.

grounding: Shows an adult coordinator noting a young volunteer move from a condescending approach to working alongside learners.

passage:
Wednesday

Clean-up drive at the lake today. Lavanya and I did three hours. I wanted to post a photo of us with the rubbish bags, and I almost did. Then I saw the fishermen's families who live there picking up plastic every morning without anyone clicking photos. I felt a bit fake. 😕

Asked one of the older men what would actually help. He said the drain from the market dumps into the lake every week and nobody listens to them. That's not something a Sunday selfie fixes.

Lavanya knows someone at the ward office. We're going to go with him next week and just listen, not take over. Maybe carry the letter he's already written.

Didn't post the photo. Felt better, weirdly.
— Imran

qa.q: Where did Imran and Lavanya do the clean-up drive?
qa.a: They did it at the lake.

qa.q: How did Imran feel about posting the photo, and why?
qa.a: Imran felt uncomfortable and a bit fake after seeing the local families quietly pick up plastic every morning, so the post seemed more about looking good than helping.

qa.q: What makes Imran's new plan more useful than the photo?
qa.a: Supporting the older man's existing effort with the ward office tackles the real cause, the market drain, while letting him lead.

qa.q: How might the fishermen's families feel about volunteers who only come for photos?
qa.a: They might feel ignored or used, since their daily work and real problems stay invisible.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer questioning their own motives and choosing to support locals' own efforts instead of seeking credit.

passage: Parveen arrived in the village near Barmer with a suitcase of donated storybooks and a plan: a reading corner for girls in the panchayat hall. On the first day, only three girls came. Ujjwal, the local schoolteacher who had invited her volunteer group, didn't say much. That evening, sitting on his doorstep, she asked why. 'The girls fetch water between four and six,' he said. 'Your timing is their work time.' Parveen felt her cheeks burn. She had planned from her college room, not from here. The next morning she went to the women at the well and asked when the girls were free. Early morning, they said, and Sundays. She moved the corner and asked two older girls to choose which books went on the shelf. By the second week the hall was full, and it no longer felt like her project.

qa.q: What did Parveen bring to the village?
qa.a: A suitcase of donated storybooks.

qa.q: Why did Parveen's cheeks burn when Ujjwal explained the timing?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, realising she had planned from her college room without learning about the girls' daily lives.

qa.q: What changed Parveen's project for the better?
qa.a: Asking the women when the girls were free and letting older girls choose the books made the corner fit the community.

qa.q: How might the older girls feel being asked to choose the books?
qa.a: Trusted and involved, so the reading corner feels like theirs rather than an outsider's.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer learning to listen to a village community and let go of ownership of her project.

passage: On his first Saturday at the community language café in Marseille, Santiago arrived with a plan: a slideshow on French verbs and a camera to "document the impact" for his university application. Nour, who had run the café for three years and had arrived from Aleppo as a teenager herself, gently took the camera. "No photos of people without asking. And no slideshow. Just sit, and let them lead." Santiago felt deflated. He sat across from an older man, Karim, who had run a bakery back home. Karim didn't want verbs. He wanted to understand a tenancy form. They spent an hour on it, Santiago mostly listening and looking up words. At the end Karim shook his hand and said, in careful French, "You are a good student." Santiago laughed. He came back the next Saturday without the camera.

qa.q: What did Karim want help with?
qa.a: Understanding a tenancy form.

qa.q: What was Santiago feeling when Nour took the camera?
qa.a: Santiago felt deflated, since his plan to document the impact had been set aside.

qa.q: What shift made Santiago's volunteering useful?
qa.a: Letting Karim lead and listening, instead of teaching a prepared lesson or taking photos, meant the help matched a real need.

qa.q: How might Karim have seen the hour with Santiago?
qa.a: Karim seems to have felt respected and helped, turning the roles around with a joke that Santiago was the learner.

grounding: A young volunteer in France drops his camera and lesson plan and learns to serve by listening.

passage: Parul joined an NGO's weekend reading programme at a municipal school in Dharavi with a folder of ideas: new games, reward stickers, a plan to "transform" Class 4's reading. On her first day Sachin Sir, who had taught there eleven years, listened politely, then said, "Start by sitting with Asma and Kiran. They're stuck on joined letters." Parul felt slightly insulted. She had come to change things. But over three Saturdays on the floor with the two girls, she noticed things her folder hadn't: Kiran squinted at the board, and Asma read better when allowed to whisper. She told Sachin Sir, who arranged an eye check for Kiran through the school. At the end of the month Parul's folder was mostly unused. Asma read a full paragraph aloud to her, whispering, grinning. Parul stopped using the word "transform" in her NGO reports.

qa.q: How long had Sachin Sir taught at the school?
qa.a: Eleven years.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when Sachin Sir sent her to sit with two children?
qa.a: Parul felt slightly insulted, having come with big plans to transform the class.

qa.q: Why did following Sachin Sir's lead work better than Parul's folder?
qa.a: Sitting closely with two children revealed real needs, like Kiran's squinting and Asma's whispering, which the teacher could act on.

qa.q: How might Sachin Sir see Parul by the end of the month?
qa.a: Sachin Sir likely sees a volunteer who listened and noticed useful things, and appreciates that she worked with the school rather than over it.

grounding: A young NGO volunteer lets go of a saviour plan, follows an experienced teacher's lead, and makes a real difference.

passage:
Dear Ira,
You start at the flood relief camp next week, so here's what I wish someone had told me last year.
I went in thinking I was there to save people. I photographed children holding the biscuits we handed out and posted them with long captions about "giving back". A woman at the camp, Shanthi, quietly asked me to delete the one with her son. She said, "He is not your story." I have never felt so ashamed.
After that I changed. I asked the camp coordinator what was actually needed, not what I wanted to do. Mostly it was dull: sorting donated clothes by size, writing names in the medicine register, filling water cans. Nobody saw it. It helped more than any photo.
So: ask first, listen longer, do the boring jobs, and never post a face without permission.
Proud of you for going.
Sunaina Didi

qa.q: What did Shanthi ask Sunaina to delete?
qa.a: The photo with her son.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when Shanthi said 'He is not your story'?
qa.a: Sunaina felt deeply ashamed, realising the posts had used people's hardship for her own image.

qa.q: What changed in how Sunaina volunteered afterwards?
qa.a: She asked the coordinator what was needed and did unglamorous jobs like sorting clothes and filling water cans, without posting faces.

qa.q: How might Shanthi have felt seeing her son's photo online?
qa.a: Shanthi probably felt exposed and hurt that her son's hardship had become someone else's display.

grounding: An experienced volunteer writes to a newcomer about dropping a saviour mindset and serving without ego.

passage:
Thanks for having me. So, I'm Yusuf, and I want to be honest about the first month, because it wasn't pretty.

I joined the evening school in the basti near our college. I came with slides. Slides! On a laptop, for children who'd been working at the dhaba all day. I thought I was the hero of the story.

Pema had been teaching there for four years. She grew up two lanes away. On my third day she said, "Yusuf, these kids already know a lot. Ask them what they know first." That stung. I sulked on the bus home.

But I tried it. Turned out little Ravi could calculate change faster than me. So I started building maths problems from the dhaba bill. The kids ran the class half the time.

Now I mostly carry the chalk and fix the fan. I stopped posting photos. It's their school. I just get to be there on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: How long had Pema been teaching at the evening school?
qa.a: Pema had been teaching there for four years.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when Pema told him to ask the kids what they already knew?
qa.a: Yusuf felt stung and a bit embarrassed, and he sulked on the bus home, because he had seen himself as the hero.

qa.q: What changed in Yusuf's volunteering, and why did it help the children?
qa.a: He began with what the children knew, like working out change, and let them run the class, which respected their skills instead of treating them as empty.

qa.q: How might Pema see Yusuf's change over the month?
qa.a: Pema likely feels relieved and respected, since the new volunteer now listens and fits into the community's school instead of taking over.

grounding: A student volunteer describes moving from a saviour attitude to humble, useful service at an evening school, guided by a local teacher.

passage:
I coordinate the relief camp at the school in our ward, so I saw Arohi every day of the flood week. I'm Lalit, and I've seen a lot of college volunteers.

Most of them arrive wanting to hand things out and get a photo. Arohi arrived and asked the women from the colony how they wanted the rations shared. They said by family card, not by queue, because the elderly couldn't stand for long. She made a list and sat at a small table with the card numbers.

On the fourth day a news crew came. The others lined up in front. Arohi carried on sorting the damp rice sacks at the back. I asked her later why she didn't go. She shrugged and said, "It's not my flood."

I don't know what she was feeling underneath. She looked tired and her hands were cracked from the sacks. She came back the next weekend to help clean the classrooms, when there were no cameras at all.

qa.q: How did the women from the colony want the rations shared?
qa.a: They wanted them shared by family card, not by queue, because the elderly couldn't stand for long.

qa.q: What might Arohi have been feeling when she said, "It's not my flood"?
qa.a: Lalit could not be sure, but she seemed tired yet steady and humble, uncomfortable taking credit for other people's hardship.

qa.q: What could new volunteers learn from Arohi's first step at the camp?
qa.a: Asking the affected people how they want help given, and then following their plan, makes the help fit their real needs.

qa.q: How might the elderly families see the change to sharing by family card?
qa.a: They would feel relieved and respected, since they no longer had to stand in long queues to get food.

grounding: A camp coordinator observes a volunteer who serves flood-affected families by following their lead and avoiding attention.

passage:
First Saturday. Afreen joins the beach clean-up in Chennai with her college club. She wears new gloves, takes six selfies with a sack, and posts, "Saving our oceans today!" By noon she is hot and bored and leaves early.

Second Saturday, two weeks later. Chandrika, who sells fish on that stretch and started the clean-up with the other fisherwomen, gives Afreen the least glamorous job: sorting plastic by type for the recycler. "The photos don't pay for the truck," Chandrika says, not unkindly. "Sorted plastic does." Afreen's face goes hot, and she sorts in silence for three hours.

Fifth Saturday. Afreen now arrives at seven with a flask of water for the sorting team. She asks Chandrika what the recycler needs this week. Her phone stays in her bag. When a new student asks where the "photo spot" is, Afreen just hands her a pair of gloves and points at the sorting mat.

qa.q: What job did Chandrika give Afreen on the second Saturday?
qa.a: Chandrika gave her the least glamorous job: sorting plastic by type for the recycler.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when her face went hot on the second Saturday?
qa.a: Afreen felt embarrassed, perhaps ashamed of her selfies, when Chandrika pointed out that photos don't pay for the truck.

qa.q: How could a club leader help new volunteers skip Afreen's first-day mistake?
qa.a: Before the first visit, the leader could explain that the fisherwomen run the clean-up and give every new volunteer a real task from them.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Afreen by the fifth Saturday?
qa.a: Chandrika probably trusts her more and feels respected, because Afreen now asks what is needed and works without seeking attention.

grounding: Over five weeks a student volunteer shifts from seeking attention to quiet, useful work led by the local community.

passage:
Wasim, before you go off to that village project, let me tell you about my first one.
I was twenty, in college, and I went with an NGO to a village in Bihar for two weeks. I was so proud. I'd brought notebooks, a camera, and a plan to "teach them hygiene". On day one I lectured the women at the well about washing hands. They listened politely. Then an older woman said, "We know. The soap costs money, and the hand pump broke in March."
I felt my face burn. I'd come to save people who were already solving their own problems.
The NGO leader told me: listen first, ask what they need, do what's asked. So for the next two weeks, I helped fill forms for the pump repair and carried bricks. I took no photos.
That's what your Payal Khala learned: go to serve, not to be seen.

qa.q: What had broken in March?
qa.a: The hand pump.

qa.q: How did young Payal feel when the older woman spoke?
qa.a: Young Payal felt embarrassed and ashamed, her face burning, realising she'd come with a saviour mindset.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Payal's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Switching to listening and doing what was asked, like helping with forms for the pump repair, because it met the village's real need.

qa.q: How might the women at the well have felt during the lecture?
qa.a: The women were probably patient but a bit annoyed or amused at being taught what they already knew.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how Payal learned to volunteer by listening rather than with a saviour mindset.

passage:
Simran volunteered on Saturdays at an evening learning centre in a basti in Ludhiana, run by Vandana, a quiet woman who'd worked there for ten years. This Saturday it poured, the power went off, and half the children didn't come.
Simran had planned a slideshow on the solar system. No power, no slideshow. She felt panicky and useless.
Vandana lit a lamp and said, "Ask them what they want to do."
Simran hesitated, then asked. A girl named Pinki said, "Teach us to write a letter to the councillor about the drain." The others nodded.
So Simran sat on the floor and helped eight children write a letter about the flooding drain outside their homes, in their own words. She didn't correct their ideas, only their spelling when asked.
Walking home in the rain, Simran thought: that was the best class she'd ever not planned.

qa.q: What did Pinki ask to learn?
qa.a: To write a letter to the councillor about the drain.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when the power went off?
qa.a: Simran felt panicky and useless, since her slideshow couldn't happen.

qa.q: What did Simran do that showed service without ego?
qa.a: She asked the children what they wanted and helped them write in their own words, instead of pushing her own plan.

qa.q: How might the children see the letter they wrote?
qa.a: They probably felt proud and taken seriously, having spoken up about a real problem in their own words.

grounding: Illustrates a young volunteer letting the community lead instead of imposing her plan, despite difficult conditions.

passage:
Minakshi and Jaya ran a monthly food drive from their Chennai college, collecting rice, dal and oil for families near the railway colony.
This month, Minakshi arrived with a ring light. "We'll do photos with each family holding the bags. For the page. Donors love it."
Jaya stopped packing. "Would you want your photo taken holding free rice?"
Minakshi opened her mouth, then closed it. She'd grown up in a house where money was tight, and she remembered hating it when a relative posted about "helping" them.
"No," she said slowly. "I'd hate it."
They changed the plan. Photos only of the volunteers and the stacked bags, with no faces from the families. They asked the colony's women's group how to distribute quietly, and followed their system.
Minakshi posted one photo: sacks and tired volunteers. It got fewer likes. She didn't mind as much as she'd expected.

qa.q: What did Minakshi bring to the food drive?
qa.a: A ring light.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when Jaya asked her question?
qa.a: Minakshi felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, remembering how much she'd hated being shown as someone being helped.

qa.q: Which changes made the food drive more respectful?
qa.a: No photos of the families, only volunteers and bags, and following the women's group's way of distributing quietly.

qa.q: How might the families feel about receiving food without cameras?
qa.a: The families would probably feel more dignified and comfortable, not put on display.

grounding: Shows young volunteers moving from a publicity-driven, saviour approach to serving with dignity.

passage:
"Okay, everyone smile!" Santosh held up his phone at the edge of the classroom.
Zubin, the learning centre's coordinator, stepped in front of the lens. "Not the kids, please."
"It's for my profile. People should see what we're doing here."
"What we're doing, or what you're doing?"
Santosh flushed. "That's not fair. I gave up my whole Saturday."
"And they're glad you came. But their parents haven't agreed to photos, and the kids aren't a backdrop."
"Fine." Santosh put the phone away, stiff-shouldered.
Later, a girl from class five asked him to check her fractions. He explained the way he had learned it, and she frowned. "Didi does it with the pizza drawing."
"Show me the pizza drawing, then."
She did. It was better than his way.
At the gate, Zubin asked, "Next Saturday?"
Santosh nodded. "Yeah. I'll bring coloured chalk. Not the camera."

qa.q: What did Santosh offer to bring next Saturday?
qa.a: Coloured chalk, not the camera.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when Zubin blocked the photo?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and defensive, flushing and arguing that he gave up his Saturday, then stiff and a bit hurt.

qa.q: What changed Santosh's attitude by the end?
qa.a: Letting the girl teach him the pizza method showed he could learn from the children, so he chose to serve rather than be seen 🙂

qa.q: Why might Zubin react differently from Santosh to the photo?
qa.a: Zubin is protecting the children's privacy and dignity, since their parents haven't agreed, while Santosh was thinking about his profile.

grounding: Shows a young volunteer moving from ego and display toward humble service.
